The answer to your question is that routine laboratory markers are not entirely useful for differentiating between non-alcoholic and alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH).

While the higher MCVs (Mean Corpuscular Volume) and AST/ALT ratios in ASH do suggest a more severe underlying liver disease, these biomarkers may not differentiate between NASH and ALDH (Alcohol-Dependent Liver Hepatitis), as they can also be elevated in other conditions.

Furthermore, studies have shown that the association between these markers is not strong enough to reliably distinguish between the two conditions. For example, a study found that men with ASH who had significantly higher AST/ALT ratios than women did not necessarily have more severe disease than those with lower ratios.

In fact, research suggests that routine laboratory tests may even be less reliable in differentiating between NASH and ALDH. This is because both conditions can present with similar elevations in liver enzymes, making it difficult to determine the cause of liver damage.

Therefore, while laboratory markers such as MCVs and AST/ALT ratios are useful in assessing liver health and identifying underlying disease, they should not be relied upon as a sole diagnostic tool for differentiating between non-alcoholic and alcoholic steatohepatitis.
